I resolved last Tuesday to cancel a subscription, and I wish to set down what followed, for the benefit of any person who may be thinking of doing the same and has not yet made his will.

The subscription had cost me nine dollars a month for three years, and in that time I had used it, so far as I can reckon, twice. It was a thing for learning Portuguese. I do not know Portuguese. I do know that the little green owl who is supposed to teach it has written to me every day since March, and that his tone has declined from encouragement to disappointment to what I can only call a settled grief.

Signing up had taken eleven seconds. I timed it afterward, out of curiosity, and out of a feeling that a man should be able to put a number to his misfortunes. Cancelling took the greater part of an afternoon. The button was not on the page where I looked for it—nor on the next page, nor on the page after, which had a picture of a smiling family, none of whom appeared to have been consulted. When I found it at last, it did not cancel anything. It asked whether I was sure, and then whether I was really sure, and then, in a smaller type, whether I would not prefer to pause my membership for a period of three months at no cost, which is the sort of offer a creditor makes to a man he intends to keep.

I declined. The owl appeared on my screen with his eyes cast down.

I confess that I very nearly gave way. A person can stand a good deal of persecution—but he cannot stand to be pitied by a bird.

In the end I wrote to the company, and received within the hour a reply of great warmth, assuring me that my feedback was valued and that my request had been passed to the appropriate team. That was five days ago. I have heard nothing since, but the owl wrote again this morning; and I notice he has begun to sign himself, in the manner of an old friend, with only his initial.
